I am 65 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County my whole life. I never went to school, but my father taught me how to read the land, and after fifty years I know what works on the North China Plain. My family has about 10 mu of flat irrigable land. I do not chase new fashions—I grow what the grain station buys and what my neighbors have proven year after year.

On my main plot of 7 mu I run the wheat–maize rotation, same as everyone in the village. In early October I rotary-till and sow winter wheat. I use Jimai 22, an improved variety from the seed shop; it gives steady yields and does not fall over. I spread about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing, then topdress urea in spring when the wheat turns green. I irrigate three times: before winter freeze, at jointing, and at grain filling. I spray twice for insects, once for weeds, and once for rust. I expect roughly 1000 jin per mu.

Right after wheat harvest in early June I sow summer maize without any tillage—I just drill Denghai 605 hybrid seed into the wheat stubble, one package per mu. This hybrid is what the dealer recommends and what most farmers here plant. I spread compound fertilizer at sowing and that is usually enough nitrogen for maize. I irrigate twice during the summer, spray three or four times for pests and weeds, and harvest in October. I expect about 1100 jin per mu.

I also keep 3 mu separate for cotton. Cotton is hard work, especially at my age, but it brings cash money that wheat and maize alone cannot match. I rotary-till in April and sow Guoxinmian, an improved variety. I apply compound fertilizer and a little urea, irrigate twice, and spray many times for bollworms—probably fifteen or sixteen times through the season. I hand-pick the bolls and expect about 550 jin per mu.

I do not buy extra potash or phosphate beyond what is already in the compound bags from the cooperative. The soil here has always yielded fine with this regime, and I trust experience more than book knowledge.
